chapter: Opinions on players and ensemble jazz
title: Johnny Wiggs and Raymond Burke assessed
summary: Rose calls Wiggs the best jazz band cornetist he ever heard and Burke a great creative genius who still needs a second clarinetist in a band.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Yeah. Yeah, I'm just wondering how you fit Wiggs into something like this.

Well, how I fit Wiggs in, I think that Wiggs, from a standpoint of band cornet, that is as a jazz band cornetist, is the best jazz band cornetist that I ever heard. That is that he plays better lead, he plays proper lead, makes it easier to put a band together. And you know, to my way of thinking, was the ideal jazz band trumpet player. I also feel that the quality of the music played by Wiggs' bands in the revival is at least as good, and in many cases better, than most of the stuff that we revere as the important collector's items of York. I think from a standpoint of musical quality, that the sessions that Wiggs and Harry Shields and Tom Brown made together are certainly among the very greatest of jazz recordings. I find that I play that stuff more at home than anything else.

Yeah, I find that, in a way, how many, I find this hard to sort out in my mind, because I'm trying to sort out all the different Wiggs's in my mind, and your opinion of the different Wiggs's, our opinions.

Well, of course I always like Wiggs better when he gets the Davenport out of the horn. And I have found that in the right kind of a musical environment he does that. It always seems to me that he plays like Oliver when he's happy and like Bix when he's mad. And I find even that interesting, and I found Bix interesting enough. But, I'm not excited by that, you know, I'm not excited by that. I'm more excited by that, you know, I'm more interested than excited by that. But of course Wiggs, you see, having gone through the original period of jazz, and then gone through the lull, it was possible for somebody like Wiggs to then reassess the whole thing, come to an intellectual understanding of what was happening, and in the process then of putting together music, have a much clearer theoretical understanding of what was happening. Mm-hm. would have. And given all that hindsight then, when you put a band together and you strip away the sentiment of the old time stuff, but base it entirely on the understanding of the music and the ability of the musicians to play their parts, I think that Wiggs put together the best jazz records that I know. Well how do you rate Ray Burke? Well, Rayman is a great creative genius. He is probably one of the most original, certainly the most original creative artist in New Orleans at this time. However, he does not fulfill the classical role of the clarinet in the jazz band, and while he is always a fabulous hand to have on a session, I always feel like you still need a clarinet player if you have Rayman.
